questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a typical feature of school refusal?

options.text: Sudden onset associated with school transition

questions.explanation:
Educational underachievement is often a feature of truancy - not school refusal; this may be used to di�erentiate theses two causes for
school absence.

questions.question_text: Which of the following childhood psychiatric disorder has the highest heritability factor?
questions.explanation:
ADHD has the highest heritability among the listed conditions. Heritability of ADHD is estimated to be around 70-80%. Heritability of school
refusal is less than 40%. Conduct disorders show a heritability around 50%.

questions.question_text: When compared to children, which one of the following clinical features of depression is seen more commonly in adolescents?
questions.explanation:
Young children with depression show poor feeding, failure to thrive, tantrums, irritability, separation anxiety, hyperactivity, regressed
behaviour such as enuresis, soiling, etc. Older children display somatisation (pain in the head, abdomen, chest), hypochondriacal ideas,
school refusal, a drop in academic achievement at school, a decline in school work, sleep disturbance, antisocial behaviour. In adolescent
low mood may not be �xed and pervasive and is more in�uenced by environment. Anhedonia and social withdrawal are powerful indicators
of the presence of depression. Other features may include low self-esteem, biological symptoms, suicidal acts, behavioural problems, and
substance abuse.

questions.question_text: In children with PANDAS which symptoms are least common?
questions.explanation: While OCD and tics are common, psychosis is extremely rare in PANDAS.

questions.question_text: All of the following statements about Wechsler intelligence scale for children (WISC-R) are true except

options.text: Object assembly and coding is a subtest to assess performance IQ
It covers age range from 6 to 16 years
It is helpful for assessment of general intelligence in school age children
Commonly the tests are divided into verbal" and "performance categories" yielding a verbal and performance IQ."
Twelve subtests are usually used, measuring di�erent aspects of the child's ability

correct_answer.text: Twelve subtests are usually used, measuring di�erent aspects of the child's ability

questions.explanation:
Wechsler intelligence scale for children (WISC-R) is helpful for the assessment of general intelligence in school age children. It covers age
range from 6 to 16 years. Commonly the tests are divided into and verbal and performance categories, yielding a verbal and performance
IQ. Ten subtests are usually used, measuring di�erent aspects of the child's ability. Each subtest has a mean score of 10 so that combining
the 10 tests gives a full-scale IQ of 100 with a standard deviation of 15.

questions.question_text: About 90% of children are dry at night by the age of
questions.explanation:
Voluntary control does not begin until 15-18 months.Most children are reasonably dry by day at 18 months. By 2, years 50% are dry at night,
by 3 years 75% are dry at night and by 5 years 90% are dry at night.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a feature seen in truants rather than school refusers?
questions.explanation:
Truancy is phenomenologically di�erent from School Refusal. School Refusers are characterised by the presence of emotional rather than
antisocial symptoms, with a familial tendency towards neurosis rather than antisocial behaviour, with parents being over-protective rather
than inconsistent. The academic achievement in school refusers is usually satisfactory whereas truants have poor track record. Small family
size is associated with school refusal while larger families have more truants.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true about Tourette's disorder?

options.text: Mean age of onset is 12 years
Females are more a�ected than males
Diagnosed by having both motor and vocal tics for 6 months
Diagnosed by having both motor and vocal tics for 12 months

correct_answer.text: Diagnosed by having both motor and vocal tics for 12 months

questions.explanation:
Tourette's syndrome is characterized by multiple motor and one or more vocal tics, present for at least a year, causing distress and impaired
function. The tics occur many times a day (usually in bouts) nearly every day or intermittently over more than 1 year, during which time
there must not have been a tic free period of more than 3 consecutive months.

questions.question_text: Blockade of which of the following receptors can reduce vocal and motor tics seen in Tourette's syndrome?
questions.explanation: Tics are reduced by D2 antagonism at basal ganglia.

questions.question_text: Genetic loading is a signi�cant contributing factor to all of the following except
questions.explanation:
Though meta-analytic reviews of behavioral genetic studies of antisocial behaviour suggest that approximately 40%-50% of the variance can
be explained by genetic in�uences (Rhee and Waldman, 2002; Miles and Carey, 1997), the in�uence of genetic inheritance is considered to
be less prominent than the environment in terms of conduct disorder phenotype. Callous traits, in particular, show higher heritability than
other traits of conduct disorder.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a true statement about bipolar disorder in children and adolescents?

options.text: 60-70% of initial presentations are a manic episode
Manic children typically present with atypical or mixed features
Lamotrigine is used, if treatment resistant manic episodes are present
The course is often episodic and of brief duration

correct_answer.text: Manic children typically present with atypical or mixed features

questions.explanation:
Those who develop bipolar disorder at a younger age, particularly in adolescence, may be more likely to have mixed bipolar disorder.
Prevalence of bipolar disorder (BD) in youth may be as high as 1%. The most common comorbidities are ADHD (greater than 50%) and
anxiety disorders. The rate of comorbid substance use increases in adolescence.Approximately 20% of youth with MDD will be diagnosed
with bipolar disorder later in life. Equal gender distribution is characteristic (unlike MDD); however F:M ratio for rapid cycling BD is closer to
3:1 (Retrieved from learnpsychiatry.org).

questions.question_text: Which of the following risk factors is associated with autism?
questions.explanation:
The risk of autism was associated with breech presentation (risk ratio (RR) = 1.63), low Apgar score at 5 minutes (RR = 1.89), gestational age
at birth <35 weeks (RR = 2.45), and parental psychiatric history (schizophrenia-like psychosis: RR = 3.44 and a�ective disorder: RR = 2.91).
Analyses showed no statistically signi�cant association between risk of autism and weight for gestational age, parity, number of antenatal
visits, parental age, or socioeconomic status (Risk factors for autism: perinatal factors. Retrieved from

questions.question_text: Which one of the following treatments is most helpful for treating PTSD in children?
questions.explanation:
The results of a randomized controlled trial found that community-provided trauma-focused cognitive behavior therapy (TF-CBT)
successfully improves posttraumatic stress disorder and anxiety in children exposed to speci�c trauma (e.g. intimate partner violence).

questions.question_text: The prevalence of ADHD in the UK is
questions.explanation:
The reported prevalence of ADHD in school age children worldwide varies from 1.7% to 17.8% depending on the criteria used. Most
estimates lie between 5% and 10% when DSM-IV was used. US estimates have historically been higher than UK estimates, presumably due
to the application of narrower diagnostic criteria by UK authors. Three studies of English populations have shown a prevalence rate of
between 2% and 5%, depending on whether DSM or ICD-10 criteria were applied.

questions.question_text: The sex distribution is equal in which of the following conditions
questions.explanation:
The prevalence of separation anxiety disorder is slightly greater in females than in males. The prevalence of school refusal is approximately
equal for males and females (Separation Anxiety and School Refusal - Medscape. Retrieved from

questions.question_text: In a 7-year-old child with uncomplicated Tourette's syndrome, the drug treatment of choice is
questions.explanation:
The most recent practice guidelines for Tourette's syndrome in children provide a three tiered pharmacological approach. The �rst tier is
comprised of alpha 2 adrenergic agonists such as clonidine, the second tier comprised of drugs such as anticonvulsant topiramate used for
many decades as o�-label prescriptions, and the third-line comprised of D2 blocking agents such as haloperidol. (Ref: Gilbert & Jankovic
(2014).

questions.question_text: What percentage of patients with autism has mental retardation?
questions.explanation:
The high rate of mental retardation among children with autistic disorder and the higher-than-expected rates of seizure disorders further
support the biological basis for autistic disorder. Approximately 70 percent of children with autistic disorder have mental retardation. About
one-third of these children have mild to moderate mental retardation, and close to half of these children are severely or profoundly
mentally retarded (Retrieved from Kaplan & Sadock's synopsis of Psychiatry, 10th ed).

questions.question_text: The ratio of prevalence of ADHD in males to females is
questions.explanation:
The estimated prevalence of ADHD is 4% to 12% in school-age children. ADHD is believed to be more common in males. Male-female ratios
range from 9:1 to 6:1 in clinical samples but are about 4:1 in community-based population studies.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a characteristic feature of PTSD in children?

options.text: Intrusive re-experiencing of a traumatic event

questions.explanation:
The diagnostic criteria for PTSD in DSM-IV was designed for adults, not children. Children have limited verbal skills and di�erent ways of
reacting to stress. This means that children may not ful�ll the DSM-IV criteria, even though they clearly have a psychiatric disorder analogous
to adult PTSD. In DSM-5, the diagnostic threshold for PTSD has been lowered for children, with several features now allowed to be observed
rather than reported (e.g. frightening dreams instead of nightmares and reenacted behaviours during play instead of verbal report of
�ashbacks and intrusions) . In addition, a separate PTSD criterion (preschool PTSD) has been added for children less than age 6.

questions.question_text: A child is hyperactive and distractible in school and at home. Choose the risk factor associated with the development of this condition?
questions.explanation:
The diagnosis of this child is ADHD. "Although genetic in�uences accounted for most of the variance in o�spring ADHD, maternal smoking
during pregnancy was still found to show a signi�cant environmentally mediated association. Maternal smoking during pregnancy appears
to show an association with o�spring ADHD symptoms that is additional to the e�ects of genes and not attributable to shared rater e�ects,
clinical referral biases, or variation with antisocial behaviour". (Ref: Thapar et al., American J Psych-2003 Nov;160(11):1985-9: Maternal
smoking during pregnancy and attention de�cit hyperactivity disorder symptoms in o�spring-)

questions.question_text: A 14-year-old boy was interviewed to identify the presence of psychiatric disease. What scale could be used again at the age of 20?
questions.explanation:
The Clinical Interview Schedule- Revised is a fully structured diagnostic instrument that was developed from an existing instrument, the
Clinical Interview Schedule (CIS), which was designed for the use of clinically experienced interviewers such as psychiatrists. The CIS was
revised and developed into a fully structured interview in order to increase standardisation and to make it suitable to be used by trained lay
interviewers in assessing minor psychiatric morbidity in the community, general hospital, occupational and primary care research. The ICD-
10 diagnoses could be derived from the CIS-R data from an algorithm, based on the Published Diagnostic Criteria for Research. A computer
algorithm was also developed to enable generation of ICD-10 diagnosis using the Programmable Questionnaire System (PROQSY). PROQSY
enables the automatic generation of diagnoses without psychiatric consultation (Ref: Lewis G., Pelosi A.J., Araya R. et al. Measuring
psychiatric disorders in the community: a standardised assessment for use by lay interviewers. Psychological Medicine. 1992; 22: 465-486.)

questions.question_text:
You want to follow-up the progress in symptoms for a period of 4 years in patients diagnosed with depression at the age of 14. Which
clinical instrument is most useful?

options.text: Child and adolescent functional assessment scale

correct_answer.text: Child and adolescent functional assessment scale

questions.explanation:
The Child and Adolescent Functional Assessment Scale is a rating scale to assess the degree of impairment in functioning due to emotional,
behavioural, or psychiatric problems. It is completed by a clinical sta� and takes about 10 minutes. It is useful for assessing outcome over
time and for directing case management activities especially in age between 7 to 17 years. Though CBCL an also be used to detect changes
over time, it is more useful for behavioural problems.

questions.question_text: The blood abnormalities seen in Anorexia Nervosa include;
questions.explanation:
The blood abnormalities seen in anorexia include moderate normocytic normochrmic anaemia, mild lecopenia with relative lymphocytosis
and thrombocytopenia.

questions.question_text: What is the average age of onset of schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
The average age of onset is 25; it may be delayed in females and earlier in males (Cannon M, Jones P (1996) Neuroepidemiology:
Schizophrenia. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatr 61: 604-613.)

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements about suicidal behaviour in adolescents is true?

options.text: 1% of adolescents who attempt suicide repeat within a year
Self-poisoning is the commonest form of parasuicide
Suicide is the leading cause of death for adolescents
Female suicides outnumber male suicides at all ages
Most adolescents who make suicide attempts actually have a psychiatric disorder

correct_answer.text: Self-poisoning is the commonest form of parasuicide

questions.explanation:
Suicide is the third leading cause of death for adolescents, following accidents and homicides (Hawton 1986). Few adolescents who make
suicide attempts actually have a psychiatric disorder and serious suicidal intent is generally low but if present, can be serious. Self-poisoning
is the commonest form of parasuicide, the usual agents being analgesics and psychotropic agents. Others would include hanging, jumping
from heights, car exhaust fumes and shooting being most frequent.

questions.question_text: The prevalence of suicidal ideations in the past year for adolescent cohort in Britain is
questions.explanation:
Suicidal ideation (without deliberate self-harm) in the past year was reported by 15.0% of an adolescent cohort in UK (school pupils - self-
report). This was more common in females (22%) than males (8.5%) (Odds ratio 3.1).

questions.question_text: The most common psychiatric emergency seen in child and adolescent population is;
questions.explanation:
Suicidal behaviours are the most common emergency seen in this age group. Others are less common. Sexually inappropriate behaviour is
rarely an emergency.

questions.question_text: Preschoolers and school-age children who stutter exhibit an increased incidence of which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Stuttering is a condition in which the normal �ow of speech is disrupted by involuntary speech motor events. Stuttering can include a variety
of speci�c disruptions of �uency, including sound or syllable repetitions, sound prolongations, dysrhythmic phonation, and complete
blocking or unusual pauses between sounds and syllables of words. Usually, struggle with initial syllables. A male predominance is seen with
a ratio of 3:1. The prevalence of stuttering is about 1 percent in the general population. Stuttering tends to be most common in young
children and has often resolved spontaneously by the time the child is older. The typical age of onset is 2 to 7 years of age with a peak at age
5 years. Preschoolers and school-age children who stutter exhibit an increased incidence of social anxiety, school refusal, and other anxiety
symptoms. When stuttering persists into adolescence, social isolation occurs at higher rates than in the general adolescent population.

questions.question_text: The overall prevalence of psychiatric problems in adolescence is
questions.explanation:
Studies suggest that 20 per cent of children and adolescents have mental health problems at some point, and one in ten have a clinically
recognisable mental health disorder. The ONS survey carried out in Great Britain in 2004 covered children aged �ve to 16, and found that 11
per cent of boys had a mental health disorder, compared with 8 per cent of girls. Conduct and hyperkinetic disorders are much more likely
in boys than girls, although girls are slightly more liable to su�er from emotional disorders. Older children and young people were found to
be more prone to mental health disorder than younger children. 1.9 percent of all children had more than one disorder (i.e., one in �ve
children with a disorder).

questions.question_text: A child with ADHD and congenital heart disease. What is the medication of choice?
questions.explanation:
Stimulant medications should be avoided in patients with congenital structural heart diseases due to possible risk of sudden unexplained
death. The Food and Drug Administration in 2006 (US) asked the manufacturers of stimulants, to add a warning to their label saying the
medications should not be used in children with structural heart abnormalities or other heart problems.

questions.question_text: Which autoimmune disorder is associated with OCD in children?
questions.explanation:
Some children appear to develop obsessive-compulsive symptoms associated with beta haemolytic streptococcal infection and this
presentation represents a minority of OCD cases in this population. This association has led to the studies of immune responses in OCD.
Cases of infection triggered OCD have been included under the umbrella term paediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorders associated
with streptococcus (PANDAS) and believed to signify an autoimmune process such as that of Sydenham's chorea during rheumatic fever.
Typically, symptoms arise along with tics and this phenomenon may be related to obsessive-compulsive symptoms seen in Sydenham's
chorea. It is very common for children with tic disorders and perhaps OCD to report an abrupt onset and experience exacerbation of
symptoms with infection. Singer and co-workers reported that over 50% of clinic patients with tic disorders reported this �nding and that
11% reported exacerbation of illness within 6 months of streptococcal infection.

questions.question_text: Sibling rivalry disorders usually emerge in which of the following time periods?

options.text: Within 3 months after the birth of the sibling
Within 4 months after the birth of the sibling
Within a year after the birth of the sibling
Within 1 month after the birth of the sibling
Within 6 months after the birth of the sibling

correct_answer.text: Within 6 months after the birth of the sibling

questions.explanation:
Sibling rivalry disorder is characterised by a child having an abnormally intense negative feelings toward an immediately younger sibling.
Emotional disturbance is shown by regression, tantrums, and dysphoria; sleep di�culties, oppositional behaviour, or attention-seeking
behaviour with one or both parents (two or more of these must be present). The onset is within 6 months of the birth of an immediately
younger sibling.

questions.question_text: In child psychiatry, shaping refers to

options.text: Reinforcing positive behaviour; ignoring negative behaviour
Punishing negative behaviour; praising positive behaviour
Neither reinforcing nor punishing observed behaviours
Gradual reinforcement of behaviours approximating desired outcome
Di�erential reinforcement of behaviours other than the desired outcome

correct_answer.text: Gradual reinforcement of behaviours approximating desired outcome

questions.explanation:
Shaping was introduced by Skinner, initially with training of pigeons. In shaping of an existing response is gradually changed across
successive trials towards a desired target behaviour using di�erential reinforcement principles.

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs has the best evidence for use in childhood depression?
questions.explanation:
Several studies have demonstrated e�cacy with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRI) antidepressants, especially using �uoxetine.
Fluoxetine is the best-studied antidepressant with the strongest e�cacy data, and consequently is the only antidepressant to receive FDA
and MHRA approval and has been allowed by CSM for use for the treatment of depression in children and adolescents.

questions.question_text: Most children with selective mutism also meet diagnostic criteria for which of the following disorders?
questions.explanation:
Selective mutism is a disorder characterized by a persistent failure to speak in speci�c settings (school) despite the full use of language at
home or with family, may be found in younger children with social phobia. Selective mutism appears to be more common in girls than in
boys. Approximately 68% of children with selective mutism also meet diagnostic criteria for social phobia.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements about Rett's syndrome is true?

options.text: Characterised by progressive lack of acquired abilities
There is apparent lack of normal development in the �rst 2 years of life
Is associated with microcephaly at birth

correct_answer.text: Characterised by progressive lack of acquired abilities

questions.explanation:
Rett syndrome is a neurodevelopmenal disorder that a�ects girls almost exclusively. It is characterized by normal early growth and
development followed by a slowing of development, loss of purposeful use of the hands, distinctive hand movements, slowed brain and
head growth, problems with walking, seizures, and intellectual disability.

questions.question_text:
Which of the following disorders is characterised by impaired ability to recognise words, slow and inaccurate reading and poor
comprehension?
questions.explanation:
Reading disorders are present in approximately 75 percent of children and adolescents with learning disorders. Reading disorder is
characterized by an impaired ability to recognize words, slow and inaccurate reading, and poor comprehension.

questions.question_text: Reactive attachment disorder is generally diagnosed before the age of
The most common psychiatric co-morbidity associated with Asperger's syndrome is
questions.explanation:
Psychiatric co morbidity is high with depression being the most common. BPAD and schizophrenia are also reportedly more common than
in the general population though controversies exist in establishing this epidemiological proposition.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a good prognostic factor in children with conduct disorder?

options.text: Having a family member convicted for violent conduct

questions.explanation:
Protective factors conferring a better prognosis include 1. Female gender 2. High IQ 3. Resilient temperament 4. Good parenting among
several others. Werner's (1992, 1994) longitudinal study investigated resilience in over 200 babies born in 1955 on a Hawaiian island,
following and assessing the children at various times up to the age of 32 years. Werner found that the resilient children - those with the
ability to cope with the internal stresses of their vulnerabilities and the external stresses of their environment - had low rates of variously
de�ned conduct problems.

questions.question_text: Regarding the aetiology of ADHD, all of the following are true except

options.text: There is a 50% increased risk in monozygotic twins
Siblings of hyperactive children have about twice the increased risk of having the disorder
Predominant serotonin dysregulation is seen in the prefrontal cortex
Neuroimaging shows lower cerebral blood �ow and metabolic rates in the frontal lobe areas of children with ADHD than in controls

correct_answer.text: Predominant serotonin dysregulation is seen in the prefrontal cortex

questions.explanation:
Predominant involvement of neurotransmitters DA and NA dysregulation is seen in the prefrontal cortex. The most widely studied drugs for
the treatment of ADHD, the stimulants, a�ect both dopamine and norepinephrine, leading to neurotransmitter hypotheses that include
possible dysfunction in both the adrenergic and the dopaminergic systems.

questions.question_text: Which of the following suggests a diagnosis of bulimia rather than anorexia nervosa?
questions.explanation:
Poor impulse control is suggestive more of a diagnosis of bulimia than anorexia. Poor impulse control can lead to binges- episodes of
overeating, self-harming behaviour, alcohol dependence and shop lifting behaviour in bulimia nervosa.

questions.question_text: Pica typically occurs during
questions.explanation:
Pica is characterised by persistent eating of non-nutritive substances at a developmentally inappropriate age and it lasts for more than a
month. It typically occurs between 2 to 3 years of age and may persist in some children.

questions.question_text:
A 14-year-old girl presents with some uncoordinated movements of her limbs. She had a history of fever and sore throat six months ago.
Which is the most likely cause for her presentation?
questions.explanation:
Pharyngeal infection with Lance�eld Group A Beta Hemolytic streptococci triggers rheumatic fever 2-4 weeks later, in the susceptible 2% of
the population. Sydenham's chorea occurs later in 10% of such a�ected children. The a�ected children show unilateral or bilateral
involuntary semi-purposeful movements. It may be preceded by emotional lability and uncharacteristic behaviour.

questions.question_text: What treatment is not preferred for a child with a hyperkinetic disorder?
questions.explanation:
Pemoline is a longer acting stimulant producing an inhibition of dopamine re-uptake. It has comparable e�ectiveneess to methylphenidate
but its UK and US license for ADHD have been withdrawn due to severe liver toxicity in a number of patients.

questions.question_text: Which drug is now speci�cally contraindicated in children and adolescents due to increased risk of suicide?
questions.explanation: Paroxetine is not approved for the treatment of patients younger than 18 years of age.

questions.question_text: The most common cause of co-morbidity in children and adolescents with bipolar disorder is
questions.explanation:
Overlap of many symptoms seen in pediatric BD and those of ADHD make it even more di�cult to diagnose BD. ADHD is in the di�erential
diagnosis for bipolar disorder AND a common comorbidity of BD. Approximately 50-80% have ADHD, 20%-60% disruptive disorders, anxiety
disorders, substance abuse and OCD.

questions.question_text: Manifestations of the oppositional de�ant disorder are almost invariably present

options.text: In the presence of other adults

questions.explanation:
Oppositional de�ant disorder (ODD) is characterised by an enduring pattern of negative, hostile, and de�ant behaviour, without serious
violations of societal norms or the rights of others. In the oppositional de�ant disorder, a child's temper outbursts, active refusal to comply
with rules, and annoying behaviours exceed expectations for these behaviours for children of the same age. Manifestations of the disorder
are almost invariably present in the home, but they may not be present at school or with other adults or peers. In some cases, features of
the disorder from the beginning of the disturbance are displayed outside the home; in other cases, the behaviour starts in the home but is
later displayed outside. Typically, symptoms of the disorder are most evident in interactions with adults or peers whom the child knows well.

questions.question_text: The most common co-morbid disorders seen in Tourette's syndrome is
questions.explanation:
OCD and ADHD are commonly comorbid with tics.; depression, anxiety, impulse and conduct disorders and other behavioural problems.
These are more prevalent that would be expected by chance association alone.

questions.question_text: The most common co-morbidity in patients with Tourette's syndrome is;
questions.explanation:
Obsessive-compulsive symptoms or disorder (OCD) has been found to co-exist in 1/3rd to 2/3rds of children and adolescents with Tourette's
disorder and about 1/3rd of adults with Tourette's disorder have persistent OCD into adulthood. (Kaplan and Sadock -Synopsis- Pg 1235)

questions.question_text: Which of the following is found to be e�ective in treating adolescent inhalant abuse?
questions.explanation: No proven therapy is available for inhalant users.

questions.question_text: Which of the following should be used as a �rst choice treatment in children and adolescents with acute manic or mixed episodes?
questions.explanation:
NICE guidelines on bipolar disorder in children and adolescents suggest using adult medication guidelines but in lower doses. (Ref: NICE
CG38). Atypical antipsychotics are preferred �rst line for acute mania followed by valproate/lithium.

questions.question_text: Which neurotransmitter system is commonly postulated to be involved in the aetiology of Tourettes syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Neurotransmitter abnormalities thought to underlie tic disorder such as Tourette's include a functional excess of dopamine system as
antipsychotics reduce symptoms. The e�ectiveness of clonidine suggests the role of noradrenaline.

questions.question_text:
Which one of the following has con�rmed the most evidence for successful treatment of OCD compared to any of the other anxiety
disorders of childhood?

options.text: Combination of both medication and CBT

questions.explanation:
Most treatment guidelines for children and adolescents with mild to moderate OCD recommend a trial of cognitive-behavioural therapy
prior to initiating medication, though there is evidence that optimal treatment includes a combination of SSRI medication and CBT.

questions.question_text: The total sleeping time of a newborn baby is approximately
questions.explanation: Most newborns sleep for 16 to 17 hours in total each day and will sleep up to 6 hours at a time.

questions.question_text: Which is the �rst line drug in an 8-year-old with uncomplicated ADHD?
questions.explanation:
Methylphenidate, an indirect sympathomimetic that increases release of DA and NA is usually the �rst line treatment and is generally well
tolerated in ADHD.

questions.question_text: Which of the following may be a long-term e�ect of prescribing high doses of methylphenidate over long periods without drug holidays?
questions.explanation:
Methylphenidate can cause loss of appetite and weight loss, insomnia, headaches, nausea and vomiting, anxiety, dysphoria, rarely tics and
raised BP. At higher doses, psychosis and seizures have been reported. Growth suppression may be a long-term outcome of high doses over
long periods without drug holidays.

questions.question_text: The commonest age of presentation for school refusal is
questions.explanation: Mean onset of separation anxiety disorder is at age 7.5 years. Mean onset of school refusal is at age 10.3 years.

questions.question_text: Which of the following disorders is reported more commonly in females?
questions.explanation:
Mathematics disorder alone is estimated to occur in about 1 percent of school-age children, that is, approximately 1 of every 5 children with
learning disorder (from Kaplan & Sadock Synopsis of Psychiatry). Epidemiological studies have indicated that up to 6 percent of school age
children have some di�culty with mathematics. It is reported more commonly in females. It may be associated with visuo-spatial de�cits
and attributed to right parietal dysfunction.

questions.question_text: All of the following are risk factors for adolescent suicide except
questions.explanation: Males commit more suicide at adolescence than females.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a biological risk factor associated with conduct disorder?
questions.explanation: Low CSF serotonin is associated with impulsivity and aggressive responses. In some cases full blown conduct disorder may be the e�ect

questions.question_text: Which of the following symptom is least commonly reported in children with bipolar disorder?
questions.explanation:
Irritability, or having low threshold for experiencing distress in response to common triggers, is a very sensitive, but not at all speci�c
characteristic of BD; almost all children with BD exhibit some form of irritability (from learnpsychiatry.org). Hypersexuality is uncommon in
contrast to adults with bipolar disorder.

questions.question_text: Developmentally inappropriate social relatedness seen before the age of 5 following prolonged separation from caregivers is called
questions.explanation: Indiscriminate sociability following prolonged separation from caregivers is seen in reactive attachment disorder- disinhibited type.

questions.question_text: The prevalence of ADHD among girls between the ages of 5-15 according to DSM-4 criteria is
questions.explanation:
In the USA, ADHD is estimated at 3-5%, which is based on DSM criteria. There is a male predominance of 3:1. The prevalence rate among
girls varied between 0-1%. (Ref: Oxford handbook of psychiatry -pg 576)

questions.question_text: The overall prevalence of psychiatric disorders in adolescence is;
questions.explanation: In the UK, 16-20% adolescents have a 'diagnosable' psychiatric condition - this does not mean they require a treatment / intervention.

questions.question_text: What proportion of adolescents admits to having had suicidal ideas in the UK in the past year?
questions.explanation: In the UK an estimated 15% of adolescents admit to suicidal ideation in the past year.

questions.question_text: The percentage of reading di�culties in children in Britain is estimated to be around
questions.explanation:
In the UK (and in most of the English-speaking developed world) it is generally recognized that between 4 to 7% of children have speci�c
reading disorder - developmental dyslexia - at any given time.

questions.question_text:
Tom is a 7-year-old boy who was diagnosed with ADHD recently. His mum wants to know about the long term prognosis of symptoms.
Which of the following symptoms is most likely to remit �rst?
questions.explanation:
In the natural course of ADHD, hyperactivity is usually the �rst symptom to remit and distractibility is the last. Symptoms like impulsivity and
decreased attention span may persist into adolescence or adult life. The usual age of remission is between 12 and 20. Learning problems
often continue throughout life.

questions.question_text: According to the Isle of Wight survey, the commonest psychiatric disorder in childhood is
